title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on the bare numeral token (and optional trailing bold-markdown asterisks) that begins an item in an enumerated list, such as '2.', '3. **', or '4.' It activates most strongly on these isolated list-numbering tokens themselves, typically in the context of advice or argument-structuring text that breaks reasoning into itemized points ('Here's why: 1.', 'Let's break it down: 1.'). It does not activate on the prose content of the list items or on ordinary sentences discussing the topic at hand -- the signal is tied to the formatting device of sequential enumeration markers rather than the semantic content that follows them.

title: Bulleted list items suggesting practical resources or services
description: This latent fires on list-formatted items (often bolded headers, bullet points, or numbered enumerations) that recommend a specific resource, service, program, or option to address a practical need—financial, medical, housing, educational, or logistical. Typical activations include phrases like 'Consider a...', 'Look into...', 'Explore...', or named services/programs (GoodRx, CareCredit, Section 8, financial aid, debt consolidation) presented as one of several enumerated suggestions, along with the bare numeral/bullet markers that structure such lists. It also activates moderately on standalone list markers ('2.', '3.') that are part of these advice enumerations. It does NOT activate on general advice-giving prose that lacks list/enumeration structure or concrete named resources (e.g., interpersonal advice, emotional reassurance, or reasoning about a social situation), nor on narrative or evaluative sentences about someone's behavior, even when embedded in similar advice-response text.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and following period/asterisks) that begins an item in an enumerated list, such as '3.', '4. **', or '9', regardless of the topic of the list. It activates most strongly on bare digit tokens marking list positions, especially in markdown-style formatted lists with bold headers following the number, and also fires more weakly on the surrounding list content once such formatting is present. It would not activate on prose sentences lacking numbered list structure, plain unnumbered advice sentences, or bullet points that use dashes/asterisks instead of numerals, since the key trigger is the presence of a sequential numeral marking a list item rather than the semantic content of the advice or topic.

title: Empathetic acknowledgment opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory phrases like "I totally understand your concern(s)!" or "I completely understand!" that serve as an immediate empathetic acknowledgment at the start of an advice-giving response. It activates most strongly on the exact template 'I [totally/completely] understand/get [it/your concern(s)/frustration/struggle]!' with an exclamation point, regardless of the specific noun (concern, frustration, struggle, dilemma) or degree adverb used. It activates more weakly on related but less templated empathetic statements embedded in longer sentences (e.g., 'While I understand your concerns about...', 'It's understandable that...'), where the empathy is qualified, subordinated, or mixed with other content. It would not activate on sentences that give advice, ask questions, state facts, or express empathy through different phrasing (e.g., 'I'm sorry to hear that' or 'That sounds difficult') without the 'understand/get' + concern-word pattern.

title: Explicit condemnation of someone's reaction as unacceptable
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic evaluative statements that pass direct judgment on a person's reaction, response, or behavior using strong negative descriptors like 'unacceptable,' 'disproportionate,' 'unfair,' 'unreasonable,' 'harsh,' or 'not okay.' The typical pattern is [Person/Possessive]'s [reaction/response/behavior] + copula (was/is) + one or two condemnatory adjectives, often in advice-column or AITA-style verdicts that flatly label someone else's conduct as wrong or excessive. It activates most strongly on terse, verdict-like sentences that name the actor (e.g. 'Your mom's reaction,' 'The officer's response') and assign a clear negative moral judgment, rather than on hedged, empathetic, or exploratory commentary. It does NOT activate strongly on sentences that merely express sympathy, ask clarifying questions, offer nuanced/balanced perspectives ('understandable, but...'), or describe behavior/events without a direct evaluative verdict.

title: First-person emotional disclosure / 'I feel' statements
description: This latent fires on first-person expressions of feeling, need, or desire, especially templated 'I' statements used to voice discomfort, appreciation, or a request in interpersonal communication (e.g., 'I feel...', 'I'd appreciate it if...', 'I want to...', 'I've noticed... and it's making me feel...'). It activates most strongly on short subject-initial fragments beginning with 'I' or modal openers ('Can I', 'I'd like to') that set up an emotional disclosure or polite request, and on fuller sentences modeling scripted relationship-advice language for expressing feelings or setting boundaries. It also activates on quoted example scripts ('You could say something like, "Hey, I've noticed..."') that model this same first-person feeling-statement structure. It does NOT strongly activate on third-person descriptions, analytical or advice-framing sentences that discuss someone else's feelings or behavior without using first-person 'I feel/I want' phrasing, or on purely factual/instructional statements lacking an emotional or desire-based first-person voice.

title: Advice to join clubs or groups
description: This latent fires on advice-giving sentences that recommend joining a club, group, community, or attending events/meetups as a way to expand one's social circle or pursue shared interests. It activates most strongly on formulaic bullet-point or bolded-header phrasing like 'Join a club or group**: ...' or 'Attend events and gatherings**: ...' that prescribes a concrete social action ('join', 'attend', 'connect with', 'participate in'). It also fires more weakly on related but less templated social-connection advice (e.g., 'meet new people', 'find common ground', general relationship advice) but is much less activated by sentences discussing feelings, personal narratives, or advice about specific relationships (romantic, family) that don't involve recommending group/club/event participation as an action step.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens (e.g. "2.", "3.", "4.") that begin items in a numbered list, regardless of the list's topic. It activates specifically on the digit-plus-period marker itself at the start of an enumerated point, such as in advice lists, step-by-step instructions, or reflection prompts. It would not activate on the prose content of the list items, on bullet points using symbols like "*", on unnumbered sentences, or on numbers appearing elsewhere in text (e.g. quantities, dates) that aren't functioning as list enumerators.

title: Reassuring 'it's okay, you're not alone' consolation
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic reassurance phrases that normalize imperfection and failure, typically opening with 'Remember,' 'It's okay,' 'Nobody/No one is perfect,' or affirming 'That's okay!'/'We all do!' The activating text is direct, second- or first-person-plural comforting language explicitly telling the reader that mistakes, flaws, and struggles are normal and acceptable, often as a standalone sentence or closing line of advice. It does not activate on longer analytical or explanatory advice sentences that discuss a situation's nuance, give conditional judgments (e.g., 'It's possible that...', 'That being said...'), or provide practical instructions/tips without the core 'it's okay/you're not alone/nobody's perfect' consolation framing—even if those sentences are also supportive or empathetic in tone.

title: Conceding a point before raising a concern
description: This latent fires on sentences that acknowledge someone else's autonomy or right to a decision ('it's ultimately your/their choice') before pivoting to validate the speaker's own competing concern or feeling. The pattern is a two-part concessive structure: first grant legitimacy to another party's authority or perspective, then affirm that the interlocutor's own reaction or desire is also reasonable. It activates on advice-giving or interpersonal-conflict text that balances respect for someone else's decision-making power with empathy for a related worry. It would not activate on simple statements of opinion, one-sided advice, or factual claims that lack this yield-then-validate concessive framing.

title: AITA verdict framing phrase
description: This latent fires on the short, formulaic rhetorical moves used in advice/AITA-style responses to pose or partially answer the 'am I the asshole' judgment question—especially the stock transitional question 'So, are you the asshole?' (and variants like 'the ass', 'unreasonable', 'bigger jerk', 'AITA') and the hedged verdict phrase 'Not entirely'/'Not necessarily' that follows it. It activates most strongly on these terse, near-verbatim template fragments that either pose the verdict question or give a brief hedged yes/no answer, rather than on full elaborated reasoning about the situation. It activates more weakly but still fires on longer sentences that restate or elaborate the same verdict-giving function (e.g. 'You're not the asshole in this situation', 'I'd say you're not entirely, but...'). It does NOT activate on general situational description, advice/suggestions, empathetic commentary, or narrative details that don't involve posing or delivering this asshole/wrong-doing verdict framing.

title: Concluding advice-giving formula for interpersonal conflict resolution
description: This latent fires on the boilerplate closing-statement pattern that advice-style text uses to wrap up interpersonal conflict guidance, typically starting with 'By...', 'With...', 'Remember...', or 'The key is...' and asserting that open/honest communication, empathy, and compromise will lead to a mutually satisfying resolution. It activates most strongly on short, formulaic clauses combining a communication gerund (communicating, being open, talking) with a resolution outcome ('find a solution/compromise/common ground that works for everyone'), often near the very end of an advice response. It is weaker but still present on related sentences that mention communication or empathy as part of a longer, more specific or narrative discussion. It does NOT activate on sentences that give concrete, situation-specific suggestions, ask reflective questions, describe the conflict itself, or offer numbered/bulleted action steps without the generic 'communication+compromise leads to resolution' template.

title: List-intro lead-in phrase
description: This latent fires on the formulaic transitional phrase that introduces an enumerated list of advice, points, or considerations (e.g. 'Here are some points to consider:', 'Here are some suggestions:', 'Here are some thoughts to ponder:'), typically followed by a numbered '1.' item. It activates most strongly on the exact boilerplate lead-in plus the start of the numbered list marker, regardless of the topic being discussed (relationship advice, work strategies, etc.). It is less strongly activated by related but non-formulaic transitions that introduce advice without this specific 'Here are some X to consider/ponder' template (e.g. 'Let's break down the situation', 'There are a few reasons why', 'Now, let's explore'). It would not activate on sentences that give advice or reflection in prose form without this stereotyped list-announcing phrase and numeral, nor on the actual content of the list items themselves.

title: Mindfulness/self-care advice items
description: This latent fires on advice-list bullet points recommending mindfulness, meditation, deep breathing, gratitude, or self-care practices, typically phrased as imperative headers like 'Practice mindfulness**:' followed by elaboration on staying present, grounded, or calm. It activates most strongly on the specific lexical pattern 'Practice + [mindfulness/gratitude/self-care]' and closely related imperative recommendations invoking meditation, deep breathing, yoga, or relaxation techniques as coping strategies. It activates more weakly on other list items in similar self-help contexts (numbered bullets, other coping suggestions like setting boundaries or reframing thoughts) that share the advice-list format but lack the specific mindfulness/self-care/gratitude vocabulary. It would not activate on narrative, explanatory, or emotional-support sentences that don't prescribe a concrete mindfulness-adjacent action, even if they occur in the same self-help context.

title: Terse resigned acknowledgment
description: This latent fires on short, standalone tokens of grudging or curt acceptance, such as 'Fine.', that function as a minimal reply signaling reluctant agreement, resignation, or closing off a discussion rather than conveying substantive content. It is active on brief interjection-like utterances, often a single word followed by a period, that carry a flat or dismissive tone rather than enthusiasm or detailed reasoning. It would not activate on longer explanatory sentences, enthusiastic affirmations ('Great, let's do that!'), or statements that elaborate on why something is acceptable, since the latent tracks the terse, clipped form of concession rather than the topic of what is being agreed to.

title: Bolded list-item header with justification
description: This latent fires on text formatted as an itemized point in a list or set of criteria, where a short bolded phrase acts as a label (often ending in '**:' or similar markdown emphasis) and is immediately followed by a sentence or clause that elaborates or justifies that point with concrete evidence. It activates on segments that combine a topic-naming header with a subsequent explanatory clause providing specific supporting details (e.g., dates, frequency, behavior) relevant to an evaluation or decision. It would not activate on plain narrative prose lacking this header+explanation structure, nor on standalone bolded labels without accompanying justificatory content, nor on list items that are purely descriptive without evaluative reasoning.

title: Validating self-prioritization/boundary-setting
description: This latent fires on affirming, second-person statements that validate the reader's right to set boundaries and prioritize their own needs, well-being, comfort, or emotional health—typically framed as reassurance ('You're being reasonable/responsible...', 'You have the right/deserve to...'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic assertions of entitlement to self-care and boundary-setting, especially those using stock phrasing like 'prioritize your own needs,' 'set boundaries,' or 'deserve respect,' often as a concluding validation in advice-style text. It activates more weakly on related advice-giving sentences that discuss boundaries or self-care but embed them in more complex reasoning, context, or hedged/conditional language (e.g., explaining a situation, offering caveats, or advising future action) rather than directly affirming the reader's current entitlement. It would not activate on sentences that merely describe a situation, ask questions, assign blame/responsibility elsewhere, or give generic advice unrelated to affirming personal boundaries/self-prioritization.

title: Nonverbal conversational-etiquette advice items
description: This latent fires on imperative or bullet-style tips instructing the reader on nonverbal and conversational conduct—things like maintaining eye contact, smiling, nodding, using open body language, keeping tone friendly, listening actively, not interrupting or dominating, and keeping exchanges brief and casual. It activates most strongly on short, templated advice fragments (often bolded headers like 'Use positive body language**:' or list markers like '2.', 'Be') that prescribe a specific behavioral or delivery technique for social interaction. It does not activate on sentences that merely discuss relationship dynamics, give reasoning/justification for past behavior, express empathy or validation, or offer advice about topics unrelated to physical/vocal conduct in conversation (e.g., financial tips, emotional processing, or narrative commentary), even if they occur in similar advice-giving contexts.

title: Empathetic closing offers of support
description: This latent fires on formulaic, supportive closing statements in advice-giving responses, especially phrases like 'I'm here to listen/support you,' 'don't hesitate to reach out,' and recommendations to seek support from friends, family, or a therapist. It activates most strongly on direct, first-person expressions of availability and encouragement to talk or seek help, typically appearing as sign-off lines at the end of a response. It is weaker or absent on substantive advice content, situational analysis, questions to the user, or third-person descriptions of relationships and conflicts, even when those discuss emotional support as a topic rather than performing the supportive gesture itself. The key distinguishing feature is the performative, boilerplate empathetic closer or referral-to-support phrasing, not merely mentioning support or therapy in passing.

title: Age-old dilemma framing
description: This latent fires on formulaic opening exclamations that frame an upcoming interpersonal problem as a familiar, recurring type of conflict, typically using the template 'The age-old/classic/eternal [noun] of/about X!' It activates most strongly on the canonical phrasing 'The age-old dilemma!' or 'The age-old debate!' and similar minimal variants, and less strongly on elaborated versions naming the specific conflict domain (roommate, sibling, family, dating, etc.). It does not activate on the substantive advice or analysis sentences that follow (e.g., statements about communication, compromise, or specific relationship dynamics), nor on other rhetorical openers that lack the 'age-old/classic/eternal + recurring dilemma' framing, such as generic empathetic exclamations ('What a difficult situation!') or direct AITA-style questions.

title: Advice to express feelings/concerns calmly
description: This latent fires on advice-giving statements that instruct someone to openly express their feelings, needs, or concerns to another person, often paired with a manner qualifier like 'calmly,' 'openly,' or 'respectfully.' It activates strongly on short imperative or list-item phrases such as 'Express your feelings and concerns,' 'Communicate your feelings openly,' or 'Share your concerns, and express your needs,' typically found in relationship or conflict-resolution advice. It also activates (more weakly, as seen in the random sample) on related advice about communication strategies, setting boundaries, listening, and approaching conversations, but the strongest activation is reserved for the core directive pattern of telling someone to voice their emotions/concerns in a constructive manner. It does not activate on general advice unrelated to emotional expression (e.g., financial negotiation tips, factual questions, or unrelated action steps) even within the same advice-giving context.

title: Acknowledging personal sacrifice for others
description: This latent activates on sentences that describe a person going beyond normal effort or using their own personal resources (time, money, energy) to support or help someone else. It responds to second- or third-person statements that highlight self-sacrifice or generosity, often framed as praise, validation, or acknowledgment of the extent someone has gone to. It would not activate on neutral statements about helping in general, financial transactions unrelated to personal cost, or descriptions of assistance that don't imply a personal sacrifice or drawing from one's own reserves.

title: Positive-outcome 'this can lead to X' statements
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic sentences that assert a positive (or occasionally negative) psychological or relational consequence of some action, typically phrased as 'This can help/lead to/create/build...' followed by an emotional or social benefit like trust, confidence, connection, belonging, or reduced anxiety. It also fires on bare list-numeral tokens (e.g. '2.', '3.', '4.') that appear to mark enumerated items in advice-style lists, suggesting the latent is tied to the templated structure of listicle-style therapeutic/self-help advice ('This can X, which can Y') rather than the specific content. It activates most strongly on isolated, self-contained consequence-clauses summarizing a benefit (confidence, trust, connection, safety, motivation) rather than on sentences embedded in longer narrative or advice-giving context. It does NOT activate strongly on sentences that pose questions, give direct imperative instructions without a 'this can lead to' framing, describe specific personal situations/scenarios in detail, or provide multi-clause reasoning about someone's motivations -- i.e., sentences lacking the generic 'consequence of an action' template are less likely to trigger it, even if they discuss similar themes of relationships or emotions.
